articles.summary: Connected Edge AI Platforms / Deployment intern Wed, 08/12/2026 - 18:14 What Is Connected Edge? Connected Edge is an architectural approach that combines local intelligence with continuous connectivity. Rather than sending all data to the cloud for processing, Connected Edge systems perform analysis and decision making close to where data is generated while remaining connected to devices, networks, enterprise systems, and cloud services. This approach enables devices to respond in real time while still participating in larger digital ecosystems. Connected Edge architectures are increasingly used across: Industrial automation Robotics Smart homes Intelligent cameras Healthcare systems Smart buildings Transportation infrastructure Enterprise IoT As AI becomes more distributed, Connected Edge serves as the bridge between local intelligence and connected ecosystems. In simple terms: Edge intelligence enables local decisions. Connected Edge enables local decisions that can also coordinate with larger systems. Why Does Connected Edge Matter? Modern connected devices generate vast amounts of data, creating new challenges for organizations that rely on real-time insights and distributed operations. Sending all data to centralized infrastructure for processing can introduce latency, increase network costs, create scalability bottlenecks, and raise concerns about privacy and resilience. Connected Edge helps address these challenges by enabling devices to process information close to where it is generated, allowing systems to respond faster, operate more efficiently, and share only the data, insights, and actions that are needed. Faster Response Times Connected Edge reduces latency by processing data close to where it is generated rather than sending every request to a centralized cloud. This allows devices and applications to respond more quickly to events, making Connected Edge well suited for real-time use cases such as industrial automation, robotics, intelligent transportation, and video analytics. Reduced Bandwidth Consumption Connected Edge decreases network traffic by analyzing, filtering, or aggregating data locally before transmitting it elsewhere. Instead of sending continuous raw data streams, Edge systems can share only relevant events, alerts, or insights, helping organizations use available bandwidth more efficiently. Improved Reliability Connected Edge allows systems to continue operating even when connectivity to the cloud or central infrastructure is interrupted. By maintaining local processing capabilities, devices can support critical functions and decision-making without relying on continuous network availability. Better Scalability Connected Edge distributes processing across devices, gateways, and local infrastructure rather than concentrating workloads in a single location. This distributed model helps organizations support growing numbers of connected devices, applications, and data streams while maintaining performance. Enhanced Privacy Connected Edge can support privacy initiatives by processing sensitive information closer to where it is generated. By reducing the amount of raw data transmitted to centralized systems, organizations can limit data exposure and better support regulatory, compliance, and data sovereignty requirements. Cloud and Enterprise Connectivity Connected Edge combines local processing with connectivity to cloud platforms, enterprise applications, and other intelligent devices. This enables organizations to share insights, coordinate actions, and manage distributed systems across Edge and cloud environments. How Does Connected Edge Work? Connected Edge works by combining intelligent sensing, local processing, and continuous connectivity. Devices collect data from their environment, analyze that data close to where it is generated, and communicate insights to other devices, enterprise systems, and cloud services. This approach enables real-time decision-making while reducing latency, bandwidth usage, and dependence on centralized infrastructure. Sense Connected Edge systems begin by collecting information from the physical world. Intelligent devices use technologies such as cameras, microphones, motion sensors, environmental sensors, biometric systems, and wireless sensing technologies to detect events, conditions, and user interactions. Connected Edge combines local intelligence with continuous connectivity, allowing devices to process data, make decisions, communicate with other systems, and coordinate actions across distributed environments. Several characteristics distinguish Connected Edge architectures from traditional cloud-centric approaches. Intelligent Sensing Connected Edge systems continuously collect information from the physical world using technologies such as cameras, microphones, motion sensors, environmental sensors, biometric systems, and wireless sensing technologies. Local Intelligence Connected Edge devices analyze data close to where it is generated rather than relying exclusively on cloud-based processing. Continuous Connectivity Connected Edge devices remain connected to larger digital ecosystems through technologies such as Wi-Fi®, Bluetooth®, Thread®, Zigbee®, Ethernet, cellular networks, and GNSS. Connectivity allows intelligent devices to exchange information with cloud platforms, enterprise systems, users, and other Edge devices when needed. Distributed Intelligence Rather than concentrating all processing in a centralized location, Connected Edge distributes intelligence across devices, gateways, local infrastructure, and cloud resources. Selective Data Sharing Connected Edge systems typically share only the information needed to support broader coordination. Context Awareness Connected Edge devices can understand environmental conditions, user interactions, operational states, and other situational factors. Security and Privacy Connected Edge architectures often incorporate security and privacy protections directly into the device and communication layers. By processing more data locally and transmitting only necessary information, organizations can reduce data exposure while helping support security, compliance, and data governance requirements. The nature of indirect tax’s involvement in M&A – and in divestitures, carveouts, restructuring, and initial public offerings (IPOs) – appears less strategic than it should be, according to a post authored by my colleague, Larry Mellon, Senior Director – Global Tax . Larry cites a BDO survey report that contains a warning for due diligence teams: “Organizations that speed through pre-deal strategy to save time face a direct tradeoff: either rush tax considerations and expose the organization to risk or miss opportunities that cannot be recovered. Both outcomes can be avoided if tax is brought into the strategy conversation at the outset.” What the 2026 M&A Boom Means for Tax Due Diligence Those strategy conversations are focused on larger deals this year. Total global M&A value is currently on pace to reach $4 trillion by year’s end, which would be the second-highest combined deal value mark in the past decade, according to PwC . The same research also projects that 2026 deal volume will lag 13% behind 2025, which indicates a rise in larger consolidations. EY Parthenon’s July M&A activity report projects that 2026 deal volume for U.S. transactions north of $100 million will increase by approximately 8%. Deal volume and value have posted the largest 2026 gains in the life sciences, media and entertainment, consumer products and retail, power and utilities, and aerospace, defense and mobility industries, according to EY Parthenon. Several 2026 M&A dynamics elevate the need for tax expertise at the dealmaking table: Larger deals have bigger tax implications: Larger transactions tend to involve more legal entities, exposure to compliance obligations in more tax jurisdictions, and, as a result, more nexus and registration requirements. Many deals are closing faster: Deals that are sourced, structured, and signed in weeks, as opposed to months, compress due diligence time frames. This makes it more important to identify all potential risks – including unclear nexus footprints, unfiled returns, and legacy tax technologies – as early as possible, ideally, during the initial due diligence that occurs before the letter of intent is signed. Large buyers have larger migration to-do lists: As large enterprises pursue M&A in a “hunt for scale,” the purchasing company’s ERP environment, indirect tax automation solution, and tax management strategy (which in many companies now requires an e-invoicing roadmap ) typically “absorb” the target’s technology and processes. This creates larger, more detailed post-integration and migration work for indirect tax teams. What Tax Due Diligence and Risk Assessment Require The tax group’s role in M&A due diligence is straightforward: identify the target’s tax risk profile. Executing that objective requires asking numerous questions: In what tax jurisdictions does the company generate revenue? Are any tax audits in process, and what financial risks do those inquiries pose? How does the company manage indirect tax exemptions? Are there risks related to intercompany transactions and transfer pricing? What tax automation is in place? That list is just a start. This Deloitte primer identifies seven overarching questions tax groups can address to help determine whether a transaction is tax-ready. Ultimately, inclusion is the first step to tax-ready transactions. Just as the tax function is central to ERP success , it is crucial to due diligence and post-merger integration success. articles.summary: 3 Prerequisites Before You Automate Subscription Billing Key Takeaways Automated subscription billing systems that run independently from collections and cash application create unbilled receivables and corrupt deferred revenue schedules. Failed payments break revenue accounting by recording income you never collected while ASC 606 schedules treat uncollected charges as guaranteed revenue. Smart dunning with automated retry logic recovers failed charges before they corrupt revenue recognition, operating as an accounting fix rather than just a retention tool. Billing automation requires three integrated layers—invoicing, collections workflow, and cash application—in one closed loop to preserve accounting integrity. Most companies treat subscription billing as purely an invoicing problem, ignoring the downstream accounting consequences when payments fail to clear. Payment failures can create DSO numbers that misrepresent reality because the billing system records receivables that may never materialize into actual cash. Automated payment update workflows that handle expired cards and declined charges help prevent subscription lapses while keeping the general ledger aligned with actual collections.
